reference.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology / palliative care guidelines
clinicalPearls: Pressure injuries are localised damage to skin and underlying tissue over a bony prominence, caused by sustained pressure often combined with shear and friction
Common sites include the sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, and occiput, reflecting where soft tissue is compressed against bone

Staging runs from non-blanchable erythema of intact skin, through partial- and full-thickness skin loss, to exposure of muscle or bone, with unstageable and deep-tissue-injury categories where depth is obscured
Prevention is far more effective than treatment and rests on risk assessment, regular repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces, skin care, and nutritional support
Validated risk tools such as the Braden or Waterlow scales help identify at-risk patients and target preventive resources
Immobility, malnutrition, incontinence, poor perfusion, sensory impairment, and advanced age are the principal risk factors
Management combines pressure offloading, wound cleansing, appropriate dressings for the wound bed, debridement of devitalised tissue where indicated, and optimisation of nutrition
Near the end of life, skin failure can occur despite excellent care, and goals may appropriately prioritise comfort over aggressive wound healing
reference.pathophysiology: Sustained pressure over a bony prominence exceeds capillary closing pressure, obstructing microcirculation and causing local ischaemia. If pressure is not relieved, ischaemia progresses to tissue hypoxia, inflammation, and cell death, with damage often beginning in deeper tissues adjacent to bone before it becomes visible at the surface. Shear forces distort and occlude vessels, and friction and moisture from incontinence weaken the epidermal barrier. Impaired perfusion, undernutrition, reduced sensation, and immobility all lower tissue tolerance and accelerate breakdown.
additionalDifferentials: Moisture-associated skin damage or incontinence-associated dermatitis
additionalInvestigations: Structured pressure-injury risk assessment using a validated scale
Wound assessment documenting stage, size, depth, exudate, and tissue type
Nutritional assessment and screening for undernutrition
Evaluation of perfusion, continence, and mobility as modifiable contributors
Investigations for infection such as wound and systemic assessment when osteomyelitis or spreading infection is suspected
redFlags: Spreading erythema, purulent discharge, or systemic features suggesting wound infection or sepsis
Deep wounds exposing bone with suspected underlying osteomyelitis
Rapidly deteriorating or new deep-tissue injury indicating ongoing unrelieved pressure
Signs of necrotising soft-tissue infection requiring urgent surgical assessment
reference.prognosis: Superficial pressure injuries can heal with consistent offloading and good wound and nutritional care, whereas deep, full-thickness injuries heal slowly and may recur. Pressure injuries are markers of illness severity and are associated with pain, infection, prolonged hospitalisation, and increased mortality, particularly in frail and end-of-life patients in whom prevention and comfort are paramount.
pitfalls: Focusing on dressings while failing to relieve the underlying pressure
Neglecting nutrition, which is essential to wound healing
Missing deep-tissue injury because early damage lies beneath intact-looking skin
Overlooking heels and medical-device-related sites during skin inspection
Pursuing aggressive healing goals at the end of life when comfort should take priority
management: Prevention through structured risk assessment using a validated scale such as Braden or Waterlow, scheduled repositioning, pressure-redistributing mattresses and cushions, and meticulous skin care
Consistent pressure offloading and repositioning as the foundation of treating an established injury
Wound management with cleansing, debridement of necrotic or devitalised tissue and stage-appropriate dressings to maintain a moist healing environment
Nutritional support with adequate protein and energy to promote healing
Moisture and continence management and optimisation of perfusion to reduce ongoing tissue damage
Treat local or systemic infection with antibiotics when cellulitis or osteomyelitis is present
Pain assessment and analgesia, including cover for dressing changes
Multidisciplinary involvement of tissue-viability nursing, dietetics and surgery for reconstruction of deep wounds
